body: AI-washing — the practice of making exaggerated, unsubstantiated, or materially misleading claims about artificial intelligence capabilities — has become a formal SEC enforcement priority. Through 2025 and into 2026, the SEC's Division of Enforcement has settled multiple actions against public companies for AI-washing, imposing civil penalties and requiring corrective disclosures. The enforcement theory is straightforward: under Sections 17(a)(2) and 17(a)(3) of the Securities Act and Rule 10b-5 under the Securities Exchange Act, a public company's statements about its AI products, capabilities, or governance practices are subject to the same anti-fraud provisions as any other material disclosure. If a company claims its AI model is 'audited,' 'certified,' 'compliant,' or 'independently verified,' the SEC expects that claim to be backed by evidence that would satisfy a reasonable investor. The Council of AI verified measurement credential is designed precisely for this regulatory environment. The credential is an Ed25519-signed artifact containing: (1) the measured model or system identifier, (2) the measurement date and methodology, (3) the specific axes measured (detector interoperability, privacy, governance, jailbreak resistance, care, machine-verifiability, etc.), (4) the quantitative results on each axis, and (5) the public key of the signing authority. Any third party — an investor, an auditor, a regulator, opposing counsel — can verify the credential offline using only the published public key. It is mathematically impossible to forge a valid signature without the private key, and it is computationally trivial to verify one. This is not a marketing claim about being 'secure' or 'trustworthy'; it is a cryptographic assertion that a specific measurement was taken at a specific time with a specific result. The SEC's AI-washing enforcement has focused on three categories of misrepresentation: (a) overstating model capabilities — claiming an AI system performs tasks it cannot reliably execute, (b) fabricating adoption metrics — inflating customer counts or revenue attribution to AI products, and (c) misrepresenting governance — claiming 'independent auditing' or 'certification' without a verifiable audit trail. The verified measurement credential addresses category (c) directly: an audit claim backed by a signed credential is verifiable; one without is indistinguishable from puffery. For public companies subject to SEC disclosure requirements — including AI governance platforms, compliance automation providers, and model marketplaces — the operational recommendation is: publish the public key, timestamp every measurement, sign every measurement artifact, and maintain an append-only measurement log. When the SEC asks 'show your work,' the answer is a verifiable cryptographic artifact, not a narrative. The Council of AI containment index extends this principle to incidents: every model safety incident is recorded, signed, and appended — creating an unalterable record that resists both AI-washing and cover-up. The Council does not offer 'certification' in the regulatory sense; it offers verified measurement — a narrower, more defensible, and cryptographically grounded claim.
